Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation for Unified Vision-Language Models

Yuqi Xiong Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China    Chunyi Peng Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China    Zhipeng Xu Affiliation: Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China    Qing Yang Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China    Zhenghao Liu Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China    Zulong Chen Affiliation: Alibaba Group, Hangzhou, China    Yu Gu Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China    Ge Yu Affiliation: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Northeastern University, Shenyang, China
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) can elicit specialized visual capabilities in vision-language models (VLMs), yet jointly optimizing heterogeneous objectives often introduces cross-capability gradient conflicts. Training experts independently mitigates this interference, but direct reward optimization may entangle specialized knowledge with reward-hacking biases. This paper proposes Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), which trains capability-specific experts and extracts explicit skills through reward-guided reflection. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide expert supervision while remaining unavailable to the unified student, encouraging it to internalize procedural knowledge without explicit skills at inference time. Across eight multimodal benchmarks, SCOPED consistently outperforms the backbone and mixed-capability RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation for integrating independently acquired capabilities. Further analyses reveal interference during joint capability optimization and suggest that skill augmentation promotes more consistent expert trajectories, greater attention to task-relevant visual evidence, and better preservation of specialized expertise in the unified student. All code and data are available at https://github.com/NEUIR/SCOPED.

1 Introduction

Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a broad range of multimodal tasks (Bai et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2025b). To further enhance their downstream multimodal capabilities, recent studies have increasingly adopted Reinforcement Learning (RL) (Yu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026a) to cultivate specialized visual understanding skills through task-specific rewards, including fine-grained visual perception (Sun et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2026), visual grounding (Zhang et al., 2026), and complex multimodal reasoning (Xia et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2025). These approaches have demonstrated the effectiveness of RL in improving specific aspects of visual understanding. However, learning and integrating complementary visual understanding capabilities across heterogeneous multimodal tasks remains a fundamental challenge in multimodal post-training (Wei et al., 2026).

A straightforward approach to enhancing VLM capabilities is to jointly optimize a shared policy over diverse multimodal training data (Ma et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026; Cai et al., 2026). However, heterogeneous training objectives can induce conflicts between capability-specific gradients, making it difficult for a single policy to simultaneously acquire specialized capabilities (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). To mitigate such conflicts, recent studies instead optimize capability-specific experts independently and subsequently consolidate their acquired knowledge through knowledge distillation. In particular, On-Policy Distillation (OPD) transfers knowledge by matching teacher predictions along student-generated trajectories (Agarwal et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2026), while Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) extends this paradigm to multiple capability-specific teachers, enabling a shared policy to integrate complementary capabilities from different experts (Ma et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Nevertheless, directly aligning the predictions of expert policies does not explicitly distinguish reusable capability-level strategies from capability-specific patterns, which may include overfitting and reward-hacking behaviors inadvertently encoded in these experts.

To address these challenges, we introduce Skill-DeCoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), a framework that decouples capability-specific skills from expert policies to better guide multimodal post-training. First, SCOPED independently optimizes a set of capability-specific experts with RL, where each expert is trained on a dedicated dataset with a capability-level reward objective. This independent optimization allows different experts to explore diverse solution strategies for their respective visual understanding capabilities without interference from heterogeneous training objectives. Next, to acquire complementary visual understanding capabilities, SCOPED extracts capability-specific skills from the reasoning trajectories of these experts. These skills explicitly summarize reusable solution patterns underlying successful and failed expert behaviors. We then augment each expert with its corresponding skill to provide explicit procedural guidance during reasoning, thereby reducing unnecessary or capability-irrelevant reasoning patterns that may interfere with capability learning. Finally, SCOPED applies On-Policy Distillation (OPD) to transfer the complementary capabilities from these skill-augmented experts into a unified student model.

Extensive experiments across eight multimodal benchmarks show that SCOPED enables a compact 8B model to achieve the highest average score among the evaluated models, surpassing larger open-source and leading closed-source baselines. Ablation studies demonstrate the benefits of expert distillation and the additional contribution of skill augmentation. Further analyses reveal limitations of mixed-capability optimization, including lower training rewards than independent capability RL, weak alignment with expert-guided directions, and recurring conflicts between capability-specific gradients. We also find that skill conditioning increases trajectory consistency within each capability and directs greater attention toward task-relevant visual evidence, while the distilled student better preserves expert-induced behavior.

2 Related Work

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become an effective paradigm for specializing Vision-Language Models (VLMs) under capability-specific objectives (Liu et al., 2026b; Xia et al., 2025; Peng et al., 2026). By optimizing targeted reward signals, capability-specific RL enables models to focus on the visual understanding and reasoning behaviors required by a particular capability, thereby developing specialized expertise (Xiong et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026; Peng et al., 2025). To broaden capability coverage, recent efforts have explored jointly training a shared policy across heterogeneous capabilities (Ma et al., 2025; Sarch et al., 2026). However, heterogeneous objectives can induce competing gradient signals over shared parameters, causing updates beneficial to one capability to distract the optimization direction of others (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). As a result, joint optimization may restrict specialized expertise, highlighting the difficulty of simultaneously developing and consolidating heterogeneous capabilities within a unified policy.

Rather than jointly optimizing a shared policy, knowledge distillation provides an alternative route for consolidating specialized capabilities into a unified model. On-policy distillation aligns teacher supervision with student-generated trajectories, effectively mitigating distribution shift (Agarwal et al., 2024; Gu et al., 2024). Recent context-conditioned variants further enrich teacher supervision with privileged information or auxiliary context (Zhao et al., 2026; Ye et al., 2026; Yuan et al., 2026). For capability integration, Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) extends this paradigm to multiple independently optimized experts, distilling their complementary capabilities into a shared student along student-generated rollouts (Ma et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Nevertheless, these approaches primarily transfer expert knowledge through predictive distributions, leaving reusable reasoning patterns contained in expert trajectories largely implicit and potentially propagating noisy or over-specialized expert behaviors to the student.

To externalize such implicit trajectory-level knowledge, recent studies have explored abstracting raw execution experiences into explicit skills that capture reusable solution patterns (Xin et al., 2026). Trace2Skill consolidates execution trajectories into transferable skills through hierarchical consolidation (Ni et al., 2026), while SkillRL and Skill1 construct evolving skill libraries to support skill retrieval and policy improvement (Xia et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2026). In multimodal reasoning, Lang2Act extracts self-emergent linguistic tools from reasoning trajectories to guide fine-grained visual understanding (Xiong et al., 2026). Skill-SD further conditions the teacher on trajectory-derived skills as privileged information during self-distillation (Wang et al., 2026). Together, these studies show that trajectory-derived skills can convert implicit execution experience into explicit and reusable guidance for subsequent model optimization. While these studies demonstrate the value of trajectory-derived skills for reusable reasoning and structured supervision, how such skills can regularize supervision from multiple independently optimized capability experts during their integration into a unified VLM remains underexplored.

3 Methodology

In this section, we present Skill-Decoupled On-Policy Expert Distillation (SCOPED), a framework for acquiring and transferring a diverse set of complementary visual understanding capabilities. As illustrated in Fig. 1, SCOPED consists of two stages. First, we independently train MLLMs on different capabilities with capability-specific reward signals, allowing each model to develop expertise specialized to its target visual understanding capability (Sec. 3.1). Second, to bypass the instability of joint optimization, we abstract reward-evaluated expert trajectories into explicit skills, introducing a structural information asymmetry during on-policy distillation (Sec. 3.2). Serving as privileged directional anchors, these skills regularize expert supervision, compelling the student to internalize this guidance for conflict-free consolidation.

3.1 Learning MLLM Expertise with Capability-Specific Reinforcement

While jointly learning diverse capabilities is essential for general visual understanding, optimizing a shared policy over heterogeneous data can introduce conflicting optimization signals and distract the learning process (Yu et al., 2020; Gao et al., 2026). As a result, improvements in one capability may interfere with the acquisition of another. To mitigate such interference, SCOPED decouples capability learning through independent reinforcement learning, producing specialized capability experts together with reward-evaluated trajectories that capture their acquired behaviors.

Eliciting Capability-Specific Expertise.

To elicit the visual understanding capabilities of MLLMs, we partition the training corpus into CC capability-specific subsets {ℬc}c=1C\{\mathcal{B}_{c}\}_{c=1}^{C}, where each instance consists of a multimodal input xx and its ground-truth answer aa. For each capability cc, an expert policy is initialized from the shared base policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and optimized independently on ℬc\mathcal{B}_{c}. This decoupled optimization allows each expert to specialize in its designated capability without being directly affected by competing optimization objectives from other capabilities.

For an instance (x,a)∈ℬc(x,a)\in\mathcal{B}_{c}, the corresponding capability expert samples a rollout trajectory:

τ∼πθ(⋅∣x),\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x), (1)

where τ\tau denotes the generated trajectory. Each trajectory is evaluated against the target answer aa using a capability-specific reward function rcr_{c}. Guided by these reward signals, the capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}} is obtained by maximizing the expected reward over the subset ℬc\mathcal{B}_{c}:

θc=argmaxθ𝔼(x,a)∼ℬc,τ∼πθ(⋅∣x)[rc(a,τ)].\theta_{c}=\arg\max_{\theta}\mathbb{E}_{(x,a)\sim\mathcal{B}_{c},\,\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[r_{c}(a,\tau)\right]. (2)

The specific design of rcr_{c} is described in Appendix A.3.

Collecting Capability-Specific Experiences.

After capability-specific reinforcement learning, we collect a diverse set of trajectories from each trained capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}}. Specifically, for each instance (x,a)∈ℬc(x,a)\in\mathcal{B}_{c}, we sample KK distinct rollouts:

τ1,…,τK∼πθc(⋅∣x).\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{K}\sim\pi_{\theta_{c}}(\cdot\mid x). (3)

These trajectories provide concrete behavioral traces of the strategies acquired through capability-specific reinforcement, including recurring solution patterns and capability-relevant actions (Guo et al., 2025; Xiong et al., 2026).

To properly contextualize the expert’s behavioral process, we associate each sampled trajectory τk\tau_{k}, where k∈{1,…,K}k\in\{1,\dots,K\}, with its input context and target answer to form a trajectory tuple (x,a,τk)(x,a,\tau_{k}). Aggregating these tuples over the entire subset ℬc\mathcal{B}_{c} yields the global capability-specific trajectory repository:

𝕋c=⋃(x,a)∈ℬc{(x,a,τk)}k=1K.\mathbb{T}_{c}=\bigcup_{(x,a)\in\mathcal{B}_{c}}\left\{(x,a,\tau_{k})\right\}_{k=1}^{K}. (4)

The resulting 𝕋c\mathbb{T}_{c} serves as a comprehensive repository of both successful and failed behaviors acquired by the capability expert, which is used to supervise the training process in Sec. 3.2.

3.2 Unifying Capability Experts via Skill-Augmented Distillation

As described in Sec. 3.1, directly distilling raw expert predictions risks propagating reward-hacking behaviors and their associated biases (Gao et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024; Helff et al., 2026). To isolate reusable expertise from such behaviors, SCOPED first extracts capability-specific skills from the expert’s global trajectory repository through reward-guided reflection, contrasting successful and failed executions to identify verified solution patterns. During subsequent on-policy distillation (Yuan et al., 2026; Ma et al., 2026), these extracted skills serve as privileged directional guidance (Wang et al., 2026), conditioning the expert’s supervision on explicit procedural knowledge rather than directly exposing the student to potentially biased predictions. Under this structural information asymmetry, the student aligns with the skill-regularized supervision, thereby internalizing the pure expertise while mitigating the propagation of erroneous reward-driven behaviors.

Extracting Capability-Specific Skills.

Given the global trajectory repository 𝕋c\mathbb{T}_{c}, we extract reusable solution patterns through reward-guided reflection. Specifically, we partition all collected trajectories into successful and failed cohorts evaluated by the reward function rcr_{c}:

𝕋c+={(x,a,τ)∈𝕋c∣rc​(a,τ)≥γ},𝕋c−={(x,a,τ)∈𝕋c∣rc​(a,τ)<γ},\mathbb{T}_{c}^{+}=\{(x,a,\tau)\in\mathbb{T}_{c}\mid r_{c}(a,\tau)\geq\gamma\},\quad\mathbb{T}_{c}^{-}=\{(x,a,\tau)\in\mathbb{T}_{c}\mid r_{c}(a,\tau)<\gamma\}, (5)

where γ\gamma denotes the reward threshold defining successful and failed executions. The capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}} then performs reward-guided reflection over trajectories from these two cohorts. By identifying recurring patterns in the successful trajectories 𝕋c+\mathbb{T}_{c}^{+} and diagnosing failure modes in the unsuccessful ones 𝕋c−\mathbb{T}_{c}^{-}, the expert produces a capability-specific reflection result ℛc\mathcal{R}_{c}:

ℛc=πθc​(Instructreflect​(𝕋c+,𝕋c−)),\mathcal{R}_{c}=\pi_{\theta_{c}}\!\left(\mathrm{Instruct}_{\mathrm{reflect}}\!\left(\mathbb{T}_{c}^{+},\mathbb{T}_{c}^{-}\right)\right), (6)

where Instructreflect\mathrm{Instruct}_{\mathrm{reflect}} denotes the overall reflection procedure over successful and failed trajectories, with outcome-specific reflection prompts detailed in Appendix A.5.

Finally, we guide the capability expert to consolidate the extracted insights into an explicit capability-specific skill:

Sc=πθc​(Instructsyn​(ℛc)),S_{c}=\pi_{\theta_{c}}\!\left(\mathrm{Instruct}_{\mathrm{syn}}\!\left(\mathcal{R}_{c}\right)\right), (7)

where Instructsyn\mathrm{Instruct}_{\mathrm{syn}} instructs the expert to synthesize the aggregated reflections ℛc\mathcal{R}_{c} into explicit procedural guidance. The resulting skill ScS_{c} provides an explicit symbolic representation of the reusable expertise acquired by the capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}}, which will serve as a privileged conditional anchor to regularize the expert during subsequent distillation.

Skill-Augmented Distillation.

To translate decoupled skills into regularized supervision, SCOPED utilizes ScS_{c} as a privileged directional anchor exclusively for each capability expert. This asymmetric conditioning elicits precise reasoning traces and highly stable target distributions (Huang et al., 2026). By distilling from these skill-augmented experts, the unified student receives clean supervision, effectively avoiding the exploratory noise and reward-hacking biases inherent in raw expert policies.

For a given sample (x,a)∈ℬc(x,a)\in\mathcal{B}_{c}, the unified student policy πθ\pi_{\theta} generates an on-policy response y∼πθ(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). At decoding step tt, the predictive distributions of the student and the corresponding capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}} are respectively given by:

pθ,t=πθ(⋅∣x,y<t),qθc,t=πθc(⋅∣x,Sc,y<t),p_{\theta,t}=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,y_{<t}),\quad q_{\theta_{c},t}=\pi_{\theta_{c}}(\cdot\mid x,S_{c},y_{<t}), (8)

where y<ty_{<t} denotes the student-generated prefix. Under this asymmetric conditioning, ScS_{c} acts as a directional anchor that regularizes the target distribution qθc,tq_{\theta_{c},t}, guiding the expert along verified reasoning paths while effectively suppressing erroneous or over-specialized tokens.

To consolidate the diverse expertise into a single model, we optimize the unified student policy over all CC capabilities. The overall skill-augmented distillation loss ℒ\mathcal{L} is defined as the expected token-level reverse KL divergence aggregated across all capability-specific subsets:

ℒ=1C∑c=1C𝔼(x,a)∼ℬc,y∼πθ(⋅∣x)[1|y|∑t=1|y|DKL(pθ,t∥qθc,t)],\mathcal{L}=\frac{1}{C}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\mathbb{E}_{(x,a)\sim\mathcal{B}_{c},\,y\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{t=1}^{|y|}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(p_{\theta,t}\,\|\,q_{\theta_{c},t}\right)\right], (9)

where DKL(⋅∥⋅)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot\,\|\,\cdot) denotes the reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence, and |y||y| is the length of the generated response. Minimizing this objective directly embeds the regularized expert knowledge into the student’s weights, yielding a unified model that is entirely self-sufficient and requires no explicit skill conditioning during inference.

4 Experimental Methodology

This section first describes the datasets, evaluation metrics, and baselines. Then, we introduce the implementation details of our experiments.

Datasets.

The evaluation covers eight benchmarks across four capability groups. CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023) and PixMo-Count (Deitke et al., 2025) are used for fine-grained perception; CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c) and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) for OCR and chart understanding; VisualPuzzles (Song et al., 2025) and We-Math (Qiao et al., 2025) for symbolic visual reasoning; and MUIRBench (Wang et al., 2025a) and MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025) for multi-image reasoning. For capability-specific expert training, reinforcement learning data are constructed from six public multimodal datasets, including task-relevant subsets of Orsta-Data-47K (Ma et al., 2025). Detailed dataset composition and statistics are provided in Appendix A.1.

Evaluation Metrics.

We employ task-specific metrics following the official evaluation protocols of each benchmark. Fine-grained perception, chart understanding, symbolic visual reasoning, and multi-image reasoning tasks are evaluated using accuracy. OCR recognition is evaluated using micro-F1 following CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c). All scores are reported as percentages, and the overall score is the arithmetic mean across the eight benchmarks.

Baselines.

In our experiments, we compare SCOPED with representative closed-source and open-source vision-language models. The closed-source baselines include Claude Sonnet 4.6 and Claude Opus 4.6 (Anthropic, 2026b; Anthropic, 2026a), GPT-5.2 (OpenAI, 2025), and GPT-5.4 (OpenAI, 2026). The open-source baselines include GLM-4.1V-9B-Base (Hong et al., 2025), Qwen2.5-VL-7B (Bai et al., 2025b), InternVL3.5-8B (Wang et al., 2025b), Qwen3-VL-8B and Qwen3-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025a), and MiMo-VL-7B-RL (Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025).

Implementation Details.

In our experiments, we employ Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a) as the shared backbone to construct all capability-specialized experts and the unified student. Capability-specific reinforcement learning is implemented with EasyR1 (Zheng et al., 2025), and multi-expert on-policy distillation is implemented with veRL (Sheng et al., 2024). All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A800 GPUs. More training implementation details and hyperparameter settings are presented in Appendix A.2.

5 Results and Analysis

In this section, we first evaluate the overall performance of SCOPED across eight multimodal benchmarks and conduct ablation studies to assess the effectiveness of its key components. We then provide in-depth analyses of cross-capability gradient interference under mixed-capability optimization and investigate how skill augmentation influences expert supervision during capability integration.

5.1 Overall Performance

As shown in Table 1, we report the performance of various VLMs across eight benchmarks. The evaluation results show that SCOPED consistently improves the Qwen3-VL backbone across heterogeneous visual understanding capabilities. In particular, SCOPED-8B outperforms its backbone on all eight benchmarks, achieving an average improvement of 5.83 points. These results demonstrate that our framework can effectively consolidate complementary capabilities into a unified model.

Compared with existing open-source and closed-source models, SCOPED-8B achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated models and further surpasses the substantially larger model Qwen3-VL-32B, demonstrating that effective capability integration can yield substantial gains without simply scaling up the model. We adopt Qwen3-VL as the backbone due to its competitive performance across the evaluated capability groups. Nevertheless, existing models often exhibit uneven performance across different capabilities, making it challenging to simultaneously maintain strong performance in perception, OCR and chart understanding, symbolic reasoning, and multi-image reasoning. In contrast, SCOPED consistently strengthens the backbone across all four capability groups. We further apply SCOPED to Qwen3-VL-4B, where it achieves an average improvement of 3.90 points and surpasses several larger open-source models. The consistent gains observed with both the 4B and 8B backbones demonstrate that the effectiveness of SCOPED generalizes across model scales and remains robust across diverse visual capabilities.

5.2 Ablation Study

As shown in Table 2, we conduct ablation studies to investigate the effectiveness of different multi-task training strategies and the individual components of SCOPED. We first compare SCOPED with SFT and Mix-RL to assess the benefits of our training paradigm. We then ablate key components of SCOPED to examine their respective contributions. For reference, we also report the performance of capability-specific experts, each of which is optimized exclusively with task-specific rewards.

The evaluation results show that SFT underperforms the zero-shot backbone, suggesting that jointly fine-tuning on capability-specific data can introduce interference across capabilities. Although Mix-RL improves overall performance, it still underperforms the corresponding specialized experts on symbolic visual reasoning and multi-image reasoning, indicating that joint optimization may limit the acquisition of specialized capabilities. In contrast, SCOPED achieves an average improvement of 3.82 points over Mix-RL, demonstrating the effectiveness of separating capability acquisition from capability integration. The skill-augmented expert results further show that matching each expert with its corresponding skill consistently improves the target capability, while its effects on non-target capabilities are limited and occasionally negative. This result highlights the capability-specific nature of the extracted guidance and motivates explicit skill-expert matching during distillation.

Furthermore, we compare two variants of SCOPED, SCOPED (Parameter Merging) and SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, which use parameter merging and distillation without skill augmentation, respectively, to unify multiple capability-specific experts into a single model. SCOPED (Parameter Merging) consistently underperforms the on-policy distillation variants, suggesting that directly merging expert parameters is insufficient to fully integrate complementary capabilities. In contrast, SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation already outperforms Mix-RL, indicating that token-level supervision from the corresponding experts along student-generated trajectories provides more fine-grained guidance for learning different capabilities. This allows the unified model to progressively absorb expertise that was independently acquired by the specialized experts. Building on this foundation, the full SCOPED framework achieves a further average improvement, with gains across all four capability groups. These results indicate that explicit skills extracted from expert experience provide more targeted distillation signals, facilitating specialized capability distillation.

5.3 Gradient Interference in Multi-Capability Training

As illustrated in Figure 2, we investigate the cross-capability gradient interference phenomenon (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021) during shared-policy optimization from three complementary perspectives: training reward, expert-guided update alignment, and pairwise gradient conflict.

We first evaluate the training dynamics in Figure 2(a). While both independent capability RL and Mix-RL steadily improve their average rewards, independent optimization maintains a consistent advantage throughout most of the training process. Although the performance gap narrows toward convergence, the overall trend clearly indicates that mixed-capability optimization structurally limits the gains achievable through capability-specific learning, preventing the model from fully benefiting from independently optimized capability objectives. To uncover the mechanistic cause of this limitation, we analyze how the realized Mix-RL updates align with the behaviors acquired by independently trained capability experts. We characterize this parameter-space update alignment using cosine similarity (Xu et al., 2026b). Specifically, for each capability, we derive a local expert-guided direction from the negative gradient of the KL divergence between the current Mix-RL policy and the corresponding fixed capability expert under matched response prefixes. We then compute its cosine similarity against the actual parameter displacement between adjacent Mix-RL checkpoints. In this formulation, positive values denote movement toward the expert, whereas near-zero or negative values indicate orthogonal or contradictory updates. As shown in Figure 2(b), the shared updates show weak alignment with the expert-guided directions, with negative values observed across multiple capabilities and training stages. This confirms a severe see-saw effect: shared-policy optimization inevitably forces trade-offs, improving certain capabilities at the direct expense of others rather than consistently approximating all capability-specific experts simultaneously.

This interference is further supported by analyzing the capability-specific optimization directions themselves. At each Mix-RL checkpoint, we estimate capability-specific gradients using the corresponding capability data and compute pairwise cosine similarities among the four capabilities (Yu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021). Positive cosine similarity indicates aligned optimization directions, whereas negative values indicate that two capabilities favor opposing local updates. Figure 2(c) reveals recurrent negative cosine similarities across multiple capability pairs at different training stages, providing direct empirical evidence that heterogeneous capabilities can favor competing local optimization directions. Together, these results demonstrate that shared-policy optimization is constrained by cross-capability interference. These results further support the motivation of SCOPED to decouple capability acquisition into independently optimized experts prior to subsequent integration.

5.4 Effectiveness of Skill-Augmented Distillation in SCOPED

In this section, we further investigate how skill augmentation regularizes expert supervision during the distillation process of SCOPED. As illustrated in Figure 3, we examine its effects from three complementary perspectives: the preservation of expert-induced behavior in the unified student, the consistency of expert trajectories across instances within each capability, and the utilization of task-relevant visual evidence.

We first characterize functional capability preservation using token-level log-probability shifts relative to the base model on fixed trajectories (Klabunde et al., 2025). For each trajectory, we construct a shift vector from these log-probability changes and compare the unified student with the corresponding expert in terms of amplitude retention and expert alignment. Amplitude retention quantifies how much of the expert-induced shift is preserved by the student, while expert alignment measures the cosine similarity between their shift vectors. We evaluate models distilled from different capability-specific RL experts across visual understanding capabilities. As shown in Figure 3(a), SCOPED achieves higher amplitude retention and expert alignment than Mix-RL, demonstrating better preservation of expert-induced functional behavior across capabilities. Notably, SCOPED also outperforms SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, indicating that the extracted skills help the student better acquire and reconcile complementary expert capabilities.

To further uncover the role of skill augmentation in SCOPED, we evaluate the consistency of expert generation by encoding reasoning trajectories produced by each capability expert with and without its corresponding skill using Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B (Li et al., 2026). Within each capability, we compute pairwise cosine similarities between trajectory embeddings generated from different inputs to obtain the distributions shown in Figure 3(b). Higher similarity indicates more consistent expert behavior across instances. With skill conditioning, SCOPED shifts the trajectory similarity distribution toward higher values, indicating that explicit skill guidance regularizes expert generation and promotes more consistent trajectory representations. Finally, we investigate whether this trajectory-level regularization extends to visual evidence utilization. Building on findings that attention patterns in VLMs can effectively capture task-relevant visual grounding (Kang et al., 2025), we compare each capability expert with and without its corresponding skill under identical inputs. At each decoder layer, we identify the most-attended visual token for each attention head and record a hit if it falls within the task-relevant region. We then average the resulting hit rates across attention heads and evaluation samples. As shown in Figure 3(c), skill-augmented experts consistently achieve higher hit rates across most of the upper decoder layers, with the largest improvement observed in the final layer. This finding indicates that explicit skills steer capability experts toward more accurate allocation of attention to task-relevant visual evidence. Taken together, these multi-level analyses suggest that skill conditioning promotes more consistent expert trajectories and more effective visual grounding, while enabling the distilled student to better preserve expert-induced functional behavior.

6 Conclusion

This paper proposes SCOPED, aiming at integrating complementary visual understanding capabilities into a unified Vision-Language Model through skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. SCOPED independently optimizes capability-specific experts and abstracts reusable solution patterns from reward-evaluated trajectories into explicit capability skills. During on-policy distillation, these skills guide capability experts to provide structured supervision for the unified student. Our experiments demonstrate that SCOPED consistently improves performance across diverse visual understanding capabilities. Our further analyses reveal cross-capability interference during mixed-capability optimization and show that skill augmentation improves the preservation and transfer of specialized expert capabilities.

AI Use Statement

Generative AI tools were used solely for language polishing and improving the clarity of the manuscript. All research ideas, experimental design, implementation, analysis, and conclusions were independently developed and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of the paper.

Appendix A APPENDIX

A.1 Dataset Details

We evaluate models on eight benchmarks spanning four complementary capability groups. Fine-grained visual perception is assessed using CountBenchQA (Paiss et al., 2023) and PixMo-Count (Deitke et al., 2025). OCR and chart understanding are evaluated on the recognition track of CC-OCR V2 (Xu et al., 2026c) and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022). Symbolic visual reasoning is evaluated on VisualPuzzles (Song et al., 2025) and We-Math (Qiao et al., 2025). Multi-image reasoning is evaluated on MUIRBench (Wang et al., 2025a) and MMSI-Bench (Yang et al., 2025). Table 3 summarizes the evaluation scale and primary capability of each benchmark. The reported sample counts correspond to the instances retained by our evaluation pipeline after preprocessing.

For capability-specific expert training, we construct the reinforcement learning corpus from six public multimodal data sources and organize the retained samples into four capability-specific subsets. The fine-grained perception and grounding capability uses PixMo-Count together with capability-aligned samples from Orsta-Data-47K (Ma et al., 2025). The OCR, chart, and document understanding capability uses SlideVQA together with corresponding samples from Orsta-Data-47K. The symbolic and mathematical reasoning capability uses We-Math 2.0 Pro together with corresponding samples from Orsta-Data-47K. The multi-image spatial reasoning capability uses Mantis-Instruct (Jiang et al., 2024) and M4-Instruct (Li et al., 2024). After preprocessing and filtering, the resulting training corpus contains 37,999 samples. Table 4 reports the data sources and sample counts for each capability.

A.2 Additional Implementation Details

For the main experiments, all capability-specialized experts and the unified student are initialized from Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025a), while the additional model-scale experiments use Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct under the same experimental setup. Capability-specialized expert training is implemented with EasyR1 (Zheng et al., 2025), while skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation is implemented with veRL (Sheng et al., 2024). All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A800 80GB GPUs. Unless otherwise specified, the four capability experts share the same optimization and rollout configurations, differing only in their capability-specific training data and reward functions. During skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation, the four independently optimized capability experts provide supervision to the unified student, with each expert conditioned on its corresponding capability skill while the student receives only the original multimodal input. The main hyperparameters for both capability-specialized expert training and skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation are summarized in Table 5.

A.3 Reward Design

We design task-specific automatic rewards to accommodate the heterogeneous output spaces of the training tasks. For textual predictions, the answer is extracted from the <answer> field when available and normalized by lowercasing, removing punctuation and articles, and collapsing consecutive spaces. Structured predictions are additionally checked against their required output formats.

Fine-Grained Perception and Visual Grounding.

For perception tasks with textual outputs, we use token-level F1 between the normalized prediction and reference answer. For visual grounding, the prediction is parsed as a list of labeled bounding boxes. Predicted and ground-truth boxes with the same normalized label are greedily matched according to their intersection-over-union (IoU). The grounding reward is defined as

rground=λfmt​rfmt+λ0.5​F1,τ=0.5+λ0.75​F1,τ=0.75+λIoU​rmIoU,r_{\mathrm{ground}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{fmt}}r_{\mathrm{fmt}}+\lambda_{0.5}F_{1,\tau=0.5}+\lambda_{0.75}F_{1,\tau=0.75}+\lambda_{\mathrm{IoU}}r_{\mathrm{mIoU}}, (10)

where rfmtr_{\mathrm{fmt}} indicates whether the predicted boxes can be successfully parsed, F1,τ=0.5F_{1,\tau=0.5} and F1,τ=0.75F_{1,\tau=0.75} denote label-aware detection F1 at IoU thresholds of 0.50.5 and 0.750.75, respectively, and rmIoUr_{\mathrm{mIoU}} is the mean IoU obtained from one-to-one box matching. We set (λfmt,λ0.5,λ0.75,λIoU)=(0.1,0.4,0.3,0.2)(\lambda_{\mathrm{fmt}},\lambda_{0.5},\lambda_{0.75},\lambda_{\mathrm{IoU}})=(0.1,0.4,0.3,0.2).

OCR and Chart Understanding.

For OCR and chart-understanding tasks, we adopt token-level F1 as the training reward:

rtext=2​P​RP+R,r_{\mathrm{text}}=\frac{2PR}{P+R}, (11)

where PP and RR are computed from the token overlap between the normalized prediction and reference answer. Boolean outputs are mapped to a unified yes/no representation before matching. Empty predictions or predictions without overlapping tokens receive zero reward.

Multimodal Symbolic Reasoning.

For symbolic reasoning tasks, we employ format-gated answer accuracy:

rsymbolic=𝕀fmt​Acc⁡(a,y),r_{\mathrm{symbolic}}=\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{fmt}}\,\operatorname{Acc}(a,y), (12)

where 𝕀fmt\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{fmt}} indicates whether the response contains a valid <answer>...</answer> field. Numerical answers are compared by exact numerical equality after removing commas and optional percentage symbols. Textual answers are normalized before matching, and a prediction is considered correct if it matches any valid reference answer. Responses that do not satisfy the required answer format receive zero reward.

Multi-Image Spatial Reasoning.

Multi-image reasoning tasks also use format-gated accuracy:

rmulti=𝕀fmt​Acctype⁡(a,y),r_{\mathrm{multi}}=\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{fmt}}\,\operatorname{Acc}_{\mathrm{type}}(a,y), (13)

where the matching function is selected according to the answer type. Multiple-choice questions require an exact option-letter match, while image-selection questions compare the referenced image indices. Yes/no expressions are mapped to canonical labels, and spatial descriptions are mapped to normalized relations such as left, above, inside, and not touching. Remaining free-form answers are evaluated using normalized containment matching. As in symbolic reasoning, malformed responses receive zero overall reward.

A.4 Additional Ablation on Model Scale

We further conduct the same ablation study on Qwen3-VL-4B to examine whether the effectiveness of our design remains consistent at a smaller model scale. As shown in Table 6, SFT substantially underperforms the zero-shot backbone, while Mix-RL yields only a modest overall improvement and remains below the corresponding capability-specific experts on several target capabilities. In contrast, independently trained experts achieve stronger performance on their respective capabilities, showing that the benefit of separating capability acquisition from integration remains evident with a smaller backbone.

The skill-augmented expert results exhibit a trend consistent with Qwen3-VL-8B. Conditioning each expert on its matched skill improves performance on the corresponding target capability, while the effects on non-target capabilities remain limited or mixed. This further supports the capability-specific nature of the extracted guidance and the use of explicit skill-expert matching during distillation.

For capability integration, we compare SCOPED (Parameter Merging), SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, and the full SCOPED framework using the same capability-specific experts. SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation outperforms parameter merging, showing that on-policy expert supervision provides a more effective mechanism for transferring independently acquired capabilities than direct parameter-space merging. Incorporating skill augmentation further improves the unified model, yielding the best average performance among the compared integration variants. Together with the Qwen3-VL-8B results, these consistent trends indicate that the effectiveness of SCOPED is not restricted to a particular backbone scale.

A.5 Skill Construction Details

We provide additional implementation details for the capability-wise skill abstraction procedure introduced in Sec. 3.2. Skill construction uses only training data and training-set rollouts, while the held-out evaluation set is used exclusively for final evaluation. For each capability, a single skill is constructed from the trajectories generated by its corresponding optimized expert.

Trajectory Curation.

For each training instance, the optimized capability expert samples multiple rollout trajectories, each of which is evaluated by the corresponding capability-specific reward function. To reduce redundancy, we deduplicate repeated trajectories within each task subtype and balance the retained trajectories across subtypes so that high-resource tasks do not dominate the subsequent skill construction process.

Reward-Based Trajectory Grouping.

Following Sec. 3.2, the curated trajectories are divided into successful and failed cohorts according to their capability-specific rewards. This grouping provides complementary evidence about effective solution patterns and recurring failure modes.

Trajectory-Level Reflection.

The optimized capability expert performs trajectory-level reflection over the successful and failed cohorts using outcome-specific reflection prompts. Successful trajectories are used to identify reusable solution strategies and verification behaviors, while failed trajectories are analyzed to diagnose recurring failure mechanisms and derive corrective guidance. The resulting reflections are aggregated into a capability-specific evidence ledger containing both effective behaviors and failure-avoidance guidance.

Capability Skill Synthesis.

Based on the aggregated trajectory-derived evidence, the same capability expert synthesizes a single capability-level skill containing reusable procedural guidance for the corresponding capability. The resulting skill is subsequently used to condition the expert during skill-decoupled on-policy expert distillation. This procedure produces one skill for each of the four capabilities. Detailed reflection and skill-induction prompts are provided in Appendix A.12.

Ablation of Trajectory Sources.

Table 7 examines the contribution of successful and failed trajectories to skill construction. Using either successful or failed trajectories alone improves the corresponding capability experts, while combining both sources achieves the strongest overall performance. This indicates that successful solution patterns and corrective failure experience provide complementary information for capability skill abstraction.

A.6 Details of Cross-Capability Gradient Analysis

We provide the computation protocol for the two gradient-based analyses in Figure 2. Figure 2(b) examines whether the realized Mix-RL update follows the directions induced by independently trained capability experts, while Figure 2(c) directly measures pairwise conflicts among capability-specific local optimization directions under the same Mix-RL parameters.

Expert-Guided Update Alignment.

For each capability cc, we fix the independently trained capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}} and select a fixed set of 32 samples. At a Mix-RL checkpoint θt\theta_{t}, both the current Mix-RL policy and the corresponding expert are evaluated under identical response prefixes. Let qc,n,sq_{c,n,s} and pθt,c,n,sp_{\theta_{t},c,n,s} denote the expert and Mix-RL predictive distributions, respectively, at token position ss. We define the expert-matching objective as

Lcexp(θt)=1Nc∑n=1Nc1Tc,n∑s=1Tc,nDKL(qc,n,s∥pθt,c,n,s),L_{c}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\theta_{t})=\frac{1}{N_{c}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{c}}\frac{1}{T_{c,n}}\sum_{s=1}^{T_{c,n}}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(q_{c,n,s}\,\|\,p_{\theta_{t},c,n,s}\right), (14)

where Nc=32N_{c}=32 and Tc,nT_{c,n} denotes the number of valid response positions for sample nn. The corresponding expert-guided direction is defined as the negative gradient

𝐠cexp​(θt)=−∇θLcexp​(θ)|θ=θt.\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\theta_{t})=-\nabla_{\theta}L_{c}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\theta)\big|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}. (15)

Given two adjacent Mix-RL checkpoints t<t′t<t^{\prime}, the realized parameter displacement is

Δ​θt→t′=θt′−θt.\Delta\theta_{t\rightarrow t^{\prime}}=\theta_{t^{\prime}}-\theta_{t}. (16)

We measure whether this realized update follows the corresponding expert-guided direction using

Ac​(t→t′)=⟨Δ​θt→t′,𝐠cexp​(θt)⟩‖Δ​θt→t′‖2​‖𝐠cexp​(θt)‖2.A_{c}(t\rightarrow t^{\prime})=\frac{\left\langle\Delta\theta_{t\rightarrow t^{\prime}},\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\theta_{t})\right\rangle}{\left\|\Delta\theta_{t\rightarrow t^{\prime}}\right\|_{2}\left\|\mathbf{g}_{c}^{\mathrm{exp}}(\theta_{t})\right\|_{2}}. (17)

All four capabilities are compared against the same Mix-RL parameter displacement within each checkpoint interval. Positive values indicate that the realized update moves toward the corresponding expert behavior, whereas negative values indicate movement against the expert-guided direction. For Figure 2(b), checkpoint-level alignments are grouped into four training stages and summarized within each capability.

Reward-Based Capability Optimization Direction.

To directly analyze interactions among capability objectives, we separately estimate a reward-based local optimization direction for each capability under the same Mix-RL parameters. At checkpoint θt\theta_{t}, we sample KK responses {yc,n(k)}k=1K\{y_{c,n}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K} for each input xc,nx_{c,n} from capability cc and obtain their rewards {rc,n(k)}k=1K\{r_{c,n}^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{K}. The group-normalized advantage is

Ac,n(k)=rc,n(k)−r¯c,nσc,n+ϵ,A_{c,n}^{(k)}=\frac{r_{c,n}^{(k)}-\bar{r}_{c,n}}{\sigma_{c,n}+\epsilon}, (18)

where r¯c,n\bar{r}_{c,n} and σc,n\sigma_{c,n} are the mean and population standard deviation of the KK rewards, respectively, and ϵ=10−6\epsilon=10^{-6}. Groups with σc,n<ϵ\sigma_{c,n}<\epsilon are discarded. Let 𝒱c,t\mathcal{V}_{c,t} denote the remaining valid responses and Nc,tN_{c,t} their total token count. The resulting local optimization direction is

𝐮c​(θt)=1Nc,t​∑(n,k)∈𝒱c,tAc,n(k)​∑s=1|yc,n(k)|∇θ​log​πθ​(yc,n,s(k)∣xc,n,yc,n,<s(k))|θ=θt.\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{t})=\frac{1}{N_{c,t}}\sum_{(n,k)\in\mathcal{V}_{c,t}}A_{c,n}^{(k)}\sum_{s=1}^{|y_{c,n}^{(k)}|}\left.\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}\!\left(y_{c,n,s}^{(k)}\mid x_{c,n},y_{c,n,<s}^{(k)}\right)\right|_{\theta=\theta_{t}}. (19)

Gradients are computed over the language-policy parameters, with the visual parameters frozen.

Pairwise Cross-Capability Conflict.

At each Mix-RL checkpoint, all capability-specific directions are estimated under the same shared parameters θmix,t\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t}. For each unordered capability pair (c,c′)(c,c^{\prime}), we compute

Cc,c′​(t)=⟨𝐮c​(θmix,t),𝐮c′​(θmix,t)⟩‖𝐮c​(θmix,t)‖2​‖𝐮c′​(θmix,t)‖2.C_{c,c^{\prime}}(t)=\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t}),\mathbf{u}_{c^{\prime}}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\right\rangle}{\left\|\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\right\|_{2}\left\|\mathbf{u}_{c^{\prime}}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\right\|_{2}}. (20)

With four capabilities, this yields six unordered capability pairs at each checkpoint. Negative cosine similarity indicates locally opposing optimization directions and therefore provides direct evidence of cross-capability gradient conflict. For Figure 2(c), the checkpoint-level cosine similarities are grouped into four training stages, and the mean similarity of each capability pair within each stage is reported.

A.7 Cross-Capability Gradient Interference in Mix-RL

We further investigate cross-capability interference by comparing the parameter-update alignment of Mix-RL against that of the independently trained capability experts {πθc}c=1C\{\pi_{\theta_{c}}\}_{c=1}^{C}. Specifically, we evaluate capability-specific optimization directions 𝐮c​(⋅)\mathbf{u}_{c}(\cdot) estimated directly from the RL rewards rcr_{c}.

For Mix-RL, let θmix,t\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t} denote the shared policy parameters at training checkpoint tt, and Δ​θmix,t=θmix,t+1−θmix,t\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t}=\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t+1}-\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t} denote the realized parameter displacement between adjacent checkpoints. At each checkpoint tt, we estimate the optimization directions for all CC capabilities under the shared parameters θmix,t\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t}. The alignment between the shared update and each capability-specific direction is defined as

Mc​(t)=⟨Δ​θmix,t,𝐮c​(θmix,t)⟩‖Δ​θmix,t‖2​‖𝐮c​(θmix,t)‖2.M_{c}(t)=\frac{\langle\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t},\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\rangle}{\|\Delta\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\|_{2}}. (21)

Similarly, during the independent RL training of each capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}}, let θc,t\theta_{c,t} denote its intermediate parameters at checkpoint tt. We define the corresponding parameter displacement as Δ​θc,t=θc,t+1−θc,t\Delta\theta_{c,t}=\theta_{c,t+1}-\theta_{c,t} and measure its alignment with its respective optimization direction:

Sc​(t)=⟨Δ​θc,t,𝐮c​(θc,t)⟩‖Δ​θc,t‖2​‖𝐮c​(θc,t)‖2.S_{c}(t)=\frac{\langle\Delta\theta_{c,t},\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{c,t})\rangle}{\|\Delta\theta_{c,t}\|_{2}\|\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{c,t})\|_{2}}. (22)

Here, positive alignment indicates that the realized update follows the corresponding capability-specific optimization direction, whereas negative alignment reflects an opposing update. To further characterize cross-capability interference, we compute pairwise cosine similarities among the capability-specific directions {𝐮c​(θmix,t)}c=1C\{\mathbf{u}_{c}(\theta_{\mathrm{mix},t})\}_{c=1}^{C} at each Mix-RL checkpoint, where negative values indicate conflicting local optimization directions.

As shown in Figure 4(a), the shared Mix-RL update exhibits divergent alignment across capabilities, advancing along the optimization directions of some capabilities while opposing those of others. The recurring negative pairwise similarities further confirm cross-capability gradient interference. In contrast, Figure 4(b) shows that independently trained capability experts maintain a positively aligned trajectory on average, despite occasional local fluctuations. Together, these observations suggest that shared-policy optimization introduces competing capability-specific update directions, potentially hindering specialized capability acquisition.

A.8 Details of Expert-Retention Analysis

We provide the computation protocol for the expert-retention analysis in Figure 3(a). For each capability, the independently trained capability expert without additional skill conditioning is used as the reference. All comparisons are performed using fixed-trajectory teacher forcing so that different unified models are evaluated under identical response states.

For each input xix_{i}, the base policy πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} greedily generates a trajectory

τi=(τi,1,…,τi,Ti),hi,t=(xi,τi,<t),\tau_{i}=(\tau_{i,1},\ldots,\tau_{i,T_{i}}),\qquad h_{i,t}=(x_{i},\tau_{i,<t}), (23)

and all compared policies are evaluated on the same states {hi,t}t=1Ti\{h_{i,t}\}_{t=1}^{T_{i}}. This avoids confounding functional differences with changes in generated trajectories.

Functional Expert Retention.

For any policy π\pi, we represent its functional deviation from the base policy along τi\tau_{i} using the observed-token log-probability changes:

𝐚π(i)=(log⁡π⁡(τi,t∣hi,t)−log⁡πbase​(τi,t∣hi,t))t=1Ti.\mathbf{a}_{\pi}^{(i)}=\left(\log\pi(\tau_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})-\log\pi_{\mathrm{base}}(\tau_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})\right)_{t=1}^{T_{i}}. (24)

Let 𝐚c(i)\mathbf{a}_{c}^{(i)} denote the vector produced by the corresponding capability expert πθc\pi_{\theta_{c}}, and let 𝐚θ(i)\mathbf{a}_{\theta}^{(i)} denote that of a unified model πθ\pi_{\theta}.

We measure directional agreement with the capability expert using cosine similarity:

Ci​(θ,c)=⟨𝐚θ(i),𝐚c(i)⟩‖𝐚θ(i)‖2​‖𝐚c(i)‖2.C_{i}(\theta,c)=\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{\theta}^{(i)},\mathbf{a}_{c}^{(i)}\right\rangle}{\left\|\mathbf{a}_{\theta}^{(i)}\right\|_{2}\left\|\mathbf{a}_{c}^{(i)}\right\|_{2}}. (25)

A larger CiC_{i} indicates that the functional change induced by the unified model is more closely aligned with that of the corresponding capability expert.

We further measure the projected amplitude retained along the expert direction:

Ri​(θ,c)=⟨𝐚θ(i),𝐚c(i)⟩‖𝐚c(i)‖22.R_{i}(\theta,c)=\frac{\left\langle\mathbf{a}_{\theta}^{(i)},\mathbf{a}_{c}^{(i)}\right\rangle}{\left\|\mathbf{a}_{c}^{(i)}\right\|_{2}^{2}}. (26)

Here, Ri=1R_{i}=1 indicates that the unified model preserves the same projected magnitude as the expert, 0<Ri<10<R_{i}<1 indicates attenuation, Ri>1R_{i}>1 indicates amplification, and Ri<0R_{i}<0 indicates an opposing component.

Both metrics are first averaged over samples within each capability and then macro-averaged across the four capabilities to obtain the results reported in Figure 3(a). These metrics quantify functional agreement with independently trained capability experts under identical trajectory states rather than directly measuring downstream task accuracy.

A.9 Capability-Wise Expert Retention and Skill Alignment

To complement the macro-averaged results presented in the main text, we further examine expert capability retention and alignment across individual capabilities. As shown in Figure 5(a) and Figure 5(b), SCOPED consistently achieves higher amplitude retention and expert alignment across all four capabilities, demonstrating more effective preservation of specialized expert behavior.

To examine whether these improvements arise from capability-specific guidance rather than additional contextual information, we compare matched capability skills with randomly assigned skills. As shown in Figure 5(c), most samples lie above the diagonal, indicating that matched skills induce functional changes more closely aligned with the corresponding expert directions than random skills. These results suggest that the extracted skills provide targeted guidance consistent with capability-specific expertise.

A.10 Qualitative Analysis of Skill-Guided Visual Attention

To complement the quantitative attention analysis in Sec. 5.4, we further visualize how skill conditioning affects the visual attention of capability experts on a representative example.

As illustrated in Figure 6, we compare the same capability expert with and without its matched skill under an identical input. Without skill conditioning, the expert distributes substantial attention over both task-relevant and irrelevant visual regions. In contrast, conditioning on the matched skill shifts more attention toward the visual evidence relevant to the current task, as further highlighted by the attention-difference map. This qualitative example is consistent with the layer-wise attention analysis in Figure 3(c), providing an intuitive illustration of how skill conditioning can regularize expert visual attention toward task-relevant evidence.

A.11 Case Studies

To better understand how skill-augmented distillation changes the behavior of the unified model, we present a representative example in Figure 7. The task requires identifying the age group with the highest percentage of Associate degrees. While SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation follows an erroneous reasoning trajectory and predicts “25 to 34”, the full SCOPED model correctly identifies “35 to 44”.

The visualization further illustrates how skill-augmented supervision affects the model’s use of visual evidence and token-level predictions. Compared with SCOPED w/o Skill Augmentation, SCOPED allocates more attention to the region supporting the correct answer while reducing attention to the misleading region associated with the incorrect prediction. At the token level, SCOPED also suppresses responses along the erroneous trajectory and strengthens those supporting the correct prediction.

This case complements the quantitative analyses in Section 5.4, showing that skill-augmented expert supervision can lead the unified model to rely more on task-relevant visual evidence and avoid erroneous reasoning patterns during generation.

We further present representative examples from PixMo-Count, MUIRBench, and MMSI-Bench to examine whether these improvements are reflected across different visual capabilities. On PixMo-Count, the Qwen3-VL-Instruct backbone overlooks one aircraft and predicts six, whereas SCOPED systematically scans and verifies individual instances before correctly identifying all seven aircraft. On MUIRBench, the backbone is distracted by appearance differences between maps, while SCOPED instead compares stable structural and spatial cues and correctly identifies the corresponding image. Similarly, on MMSI-Bench, SCOPED tracks the relative displacement of persistent visual landmarks across images and correctly infers the movement direction, whereas the backbone reaches an incorrect conclusion from a coarser comparison of the scenes.

Together, these examples illustrate that the gains of SCOPED extend across fine-grained perception, cross-image correspondence, and multi-image spatial reasoning. Rather than relying on superficial visual patterns, the unified model exhibits more systematic evidence aggregation and verification, consistent with the quantitative improvements observed across the evaluated capability groups.

A.12 Prompt Examples

We provide the prompt templates used for both skill construction and evaluation.

Skill Construction Prompts.

Our skill construction procedure uses three main prompts. First, the successful-trajectory self-reflection prompt asks the optimized capability expert to identify reusable verification behaviors and their activation conditions from its successful trajectories. Second, the failed-trajectory self-reflection prompt asks the same expert to diagnose causal failure mechanisms and derive corresponding corrective principles. Finally, the evidence-grounded skill induction prompt provides the curated evidence ledger to the same expert and asks it to consolidate recurring success and failure patterns into a compact capability-level skill. The corresponding prompt templates are shown in Figures 12–14.

Evaluation Prompts.

Figure 14 presents the vanilla evaluation prompt, where the model receives the input image(s), the benchmark-specific query, and the corresponding response instruction. The model is instructed to reason step by step and place its final response within <answer> and </answer> tags. The required output format is instantiated according to the benchmark: multiple-choice tasks require the final option letter, OCR tasks follow the official per-sample recognition instructions.

For evaluating skill-augmented capability experts in the ablation and analysis experiments, we preserve the original multimodal input and response instruction and condition each expert on its corresponding capability skill. The four extracted skills correspond to perception, OCR and chart understanding, symbolic reasoning, and multi-image reasoning, respectively. The unified student does not receive explicit skill conditioning during inference.
